cuts.raw_narration: Inside a small wooden house on Whale Island, a boy with spiky black-green hair, Gon, is on the floor while his orange-haired aunt Mito, in a red jacket and white apron, warns him being a Hunter is dangerous and that his own father chose it over him. Gon looks down, then snaps his head up wide-eyed, jumps to his feet with clenched fists, and tells her that is exactly why he has to go — he wants to understand why the Hunter's life mattered more to his dad than staying with him.

Outside under a bright blue sky, Gon has walked a little way down the dirt path and turned back to Mito, who stands by the door with his grandmother. Instead of celebrating his promise, Mito quietly asks him to just come home safe, lifts her little finger, and Gon hooks his own pinky around hers against the sky as they seal it with the childhood chant about a thousand needles.

The scene jumps to a ship's cabin at sea. A bearded old captain with a pipe is quizzing the last three passengers still on their feet. Gon tells him plainly that his father is a Hunter and that being a Hunter was the most important thing in the world to his dad — that is why he left Whale Island. The captain's eyes narrow through the smoke and he mutters that this is Ging's son, and that the day has come at last.

Beside Gon are a loud young man in a blue suit and round glasses called Leorio, and a calm blond youth in a blue-and-red tabard called Kurapika. The captain, still on his pipe, tells them the Hunter Exam has already started — he has washed out every other passenger, dozens of them groaning on bunks below deck — and the only way these three move on is if he personally gives the go-ahead.

Kurapika answers first. In front of a wall map he says he is the sole survivor of the Kurta clan, that four years ago his entire people were annihilated by criminals, and that he wants to become a Hunter to capture the Phantom Troupe. The captain warns him it is a suicide mission. Kurapika replies that the one thing he fears is that time will quiet the rage in his heart, and as he says it the camera pushes in on his eye, which flashes a vivid scarlet red before he closes it again.

When it is Leorio's turn the mood snaps the other way. Grinning, he says his reason is simple — money — and the cabin dissolves into his fantasy of a pink storybook mansion, a gleaming gold sports car, Leorio in red sunglasses cackling among floating bottles of liquor. From behind him Kurapika, eyes still shut, cuts in, "If only you could buy class as well, Leorio." Leorio's face goes red with rage and he stalks toward the door telling Kurapika to step outside so he can finish off the filthy Kurta bloodline once and for all.

With the two of them squared off outside, Gon spots something through the cabin window: in the pitch-black storm a towering waterspout is spinning down out of the clouds toward the ship. The captain seizes the wheel, the crew shouts to lower the sails, and Gon bolts out into the rain to help.

The storm passes. On a now-sunny deck against a blue ocean, a sailor in a blue bandana — the crewman the three of them helped rescue — bows deeply and tells them they saved his life. Leorio, embarrassed, waves it off and mutters an apology of his own; Kurapika quietly takes back what he said and tells Leorio to drop the "Mr." — plain Leorio is fine.

The bearded captain climbs the steps onto the sunny deck, looks the three of them over, and grins around his pipe. Because they have grown on him, he says, he will drop them off at the port closest to the exam site — and then congratulates them: they are all moving on. Over a final shot of Gon on the deck the narrator says this is how Gon at last began his journey to do what his father did before him and become a Hunter.
